subject: Some changes for next version of Shiny

messages.author: 55771919c42cb6a1
messages.subject: Some changes for next version of Shiny
parts:
Hi everyone -

We've made some changes for the next release of Shiny. There are two big changes from Shiny 0.2.4. The first is that reactive functions are now lazily evaluated. (Note that this is distinct from R's lazy evaluation.) What this means for you, as a developer, is that reactive functions will be evaluated more efficiently. You may have noticed that sometimes reactive functions are run multiple times, even when they really only need to be run once. The switch to lazy evaluation should reduce the number of times that reactive functions are run, resulting in a more efficient use of resources.


The other major change is that we've added something called a reactive values object. You can use a reactive values object for storing intermediate values -- ones that take a value from `input` and which will be used for `output`. This is especially useful if calculating the intermediate value takes a lot of time, and is used by multiple reactive outputs: you can calculate a reactive value once, and then use it in multiple reactive outputs.


For any of of you who have already used the reactiveValue() function that was in development, please note that there's a major change in how it's used. This is the old way, which no longer works:
  # Create the value
  valueA <- reactiveValue(10)
  # Read the value
  value(valueA)
  # Write to the value
  value(valueA) <- 20

The new syntax should feel much more natural for R users. The new way is to create an object which is similar to `input`, and then access its members, like this:
  # Create the reactive values object
  values <- reactiveValues()
  values$A <- 10
  # Another option: create the object with an initialized value
  values <- reactiveValues(A=10)
  # Read the value
  values$A
  # Write to the value
  values$A <- 20


If you want to use these features, install the development version of Shiny on your local machine and give us feedback. We'll release the new version of Shiny to CRAN soon, and once we do, we'll update Glimmer to use it.

To install the latest development version, run the following:
    install.packages('devtools')
    library(devtools)
    install_github('shiny', 'rstudio')

Then restart R.

Enjoy!
-Winston

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Some changes for next version of Shiny
parts:
Hm, this is interesting. It looks like the problem is happening because your ggplot call uses jitter. In your plot.compareMeans function, you're doing something similar to this:
  print(ggplot(dat, aes_string(x=xvar, y=yvar)) +
    geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter())

If you take out the geom_jitter(), it no longer keeps running the same plot over and over again.

You can even replace the plot with this, and it'll keep running repeatedly:
  print(qplot(1:3, runif(3)))


In both cases, if you make it deterministic by putting set.seed(44) just before the ggplot, it runs only once. I'll look into this.

-Winston

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Some changes for next version of Shiny
parts:
Hi Vincent -

One of the reasons that it was getting confused is because of this line:
    plotOutput("plots", height = 1200)

plotOutput() expected height to be a string that gets passed directly through to the web page. The issue is that the web page expects this string to have "px" at the end, like "1200px".

Because the height wasn't properly set, the web browser uses "height: auto". This was part of a reload loop: as the image loads, the browser thinks the image has almost no height (20 pixels in my browser); and then once the image is loaded, it thinks the image is 600 pixels high, as specified in output$plots. Each time the height changes, the web browser requests a new image from the server, and it just keeps looping.

In the development version of Shiny, we've made it accept a number like height=1200, or a string with "px" like height="1200px", so your existing code should run.



Another thing: in your code you use as.list(input), which is a heavyweight operation. When you call that from a reactive function, that function now depends on every single object in input. So if any input object changes, that reactive function will be invalidated and will need to re-execute. Because this is a large dependency, I would suggest not using as.list(input), and instead accessing just the objects that you need from input.

We know that as.list() is a natural idiom to use for R programmers, and in the future we're going to make some changes to make it more clear when you want to take a dependency on all input objects.

-Winston
